content: Erythrulose, also referred to as D-erythrulose, is a carbohydrate classified as a tetrose, with the molecular formula C4H8O4. It contains a single ketone group, placing it within the ketose family of sugars. This compound is commonly utilized in self-tanning cosmetic products, often in combination with dihydroxyacetone (DHA). Erythrulose is a naturally derived keto-sugar that interacts with amino acids present in keratin, a protein found in the outermost layer of the skin, specifically the stratum corneum of the epidermis. This reaction is non-toxic and results in a temporary browning effect on the skin, which is chemically similar to the Maillard reaction. Unlike a stain or dye, this process involves a chemical reaction that alters the color of the treated skin. The browning effect is analogous to the discoloration observed when a cut apple is exposed to oxygen. The resulting tan resembles the appearance of a UV-induced suntan. Due to the natural exfoliation process of the skin, where thousands of dead skin cells are shed daily, the tan produced by erythrulose is temporary. Typically, the tan lasts between 2 to 10 days, depending on the method of application and the condition of the skin. Erythrulose is a clear to pale yellowish liquid that naturally occurs in red raspberries. According to the manufacturer Centerchem, Inc., erythrulose is produced through the aerobic fermentation of the bacterium Gluconobacter, followed by an extensive multi-step purification process. Erythrulose and DHA share similar chemical compositions and react in comparable ways on the skin's surface. However, erythrulose produces a lighter and more gradually developing tan, requiring 24 to 48 hours for full development. When used alone, the tan fades more quickly than one produced by DHA-based products. Some individuals perceive the final tone of an erythrulose tan to be slightly redder and less bronze compared to a DHA-based tan. Additionally, erythrulose may be less drying to the skin, contributing to a smoother fading process. When combined with DHA, the resulting sunless tan is reported to last longer, fade more evenly, and provide a more cosmetically appealing color tone. In sunless tanning products, erythrulose is typically included at concentrations ranging from 1% to 3%. However, not all users develop a tan coloration from erythrulose, and some may experience uneven or blotchy fading when this ingredient is used. Due to the additional cost associated with erythrulose, some manufacturers consider it an inefficient additive for sunless tanning products. For individuals sensitive to DHA, erythrulose may serve as a safer alternative for self-tanning. However, erythrulose is more expensive and less readily available. Because of the chemical similarities between DHA and erythrulose, it is not uncommon for individuals to exhibit sensitivity to both compounds. Erythrulose acts on the skin's surface and does not appear to penetrate beyond the outermost dead skin layers. Side effects are generally limited to occasional cases of contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals. In many instances of suspected sensitivity, the reaction is attributed to other ingredients in the self-tanning product, such as preservatives, dyes, fragrances, or plant-based additives and extracts. Although erythrulose appears to be safe for use based on available evidence, it has not been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a self-tanning agent.
